title: XVIII: A Flood of Sunshine

teacherSummary.text: Dimmesdale decides to flee. Hester unfastens the letter and throws it toward the brook, lets down her hair, and sunshine floods the forest. The narrator warns that she has wandered in a moral wilderness. Hester calls Pearl to meet her father.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “she undid the clasp that fastened the scarlet letter, and, taking it from her bosom, threw it to a distance among the withered leaves” slowly and put it in my own words: Hester unfastens the scarlet letter and throws it away among the dead leaves. Next, craft. I notice the careful steps of undoing the clasp, then a sudden throw, like shedding a weight. The strongest word is “withered”: the dead leaves suggest the letter belongs with what is past and dying. Then, effect. What does Hester's act in the forest mean? My answer: In the forest, outside the town's law, Hester frees herself for a moment; the sunshine that follows shows how much the letter had darkened her life.

followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

items.text: How does “XVIII: A Flood of Sunshine” build on “XVII: The Pastor and His Parishioner”? Name one link of cause and effect.

items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The forest sets Hester free but the narrator questions that freedom. Useful evidence: “Such was the sympathy of Nature—that wild, heathen Nature of the forest, never subjugated by human law, nor illumined by higher truth—with the bliss of these two spirits” (XVIII: A Flood of Sunshine, paragraph 13): Nature's response. Theme link: nature responds to their happiness. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
